sections.heading: Locating roots by a change of sign

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=x^3-4x-2$ has a root between $x=2$ and $x=3$.
questions.answer: $f(2)=8-8-2=-2$. $f(3)=27-12-2=13$. Since $f(2)<0$ and $f(3)>0$, the sign change confirms a root lies in $(2,3)$.

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=x^3-x-1$ has a root between $x=1$ and $x=2$.
questions.answer: $f(1)=1-1-1=-1$. $f(2)=8-2-1=5$. Since $f(1)<0$ and $f(2)>0$, the sign change confirms a root lies in $(1,2)$.

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=\ln x-2+x$ has a root between $x=1$ and $x=2$.
questions.answer: $f(1)=\ln1-2+1=-1$. $f(2)=\ln2-2+2=\ln2\approx0.693$. Since $f(1)<0$ and $f(2)>0$, the sign change confirms a root lies in $(1,2)$.

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=x^3-2x-5$ has a root between $x=2$ and $x=3$.
questions.answer: $f(2)=8-4-5=-1$. $f(3)=27-6-5=16$. Since $f(2)<0$ and $f(3)>0$, the sign change confirms a root lies in $(2,3)$.

questions.q: Using $f(x)=x^3-x-1$, which changes sign between $x=1$ and $x=2$, evaluate $f(1.5)$ and give a narrower interval containing the root.
Continuing from the previous problem, evaluate $f(1.25)$ and give a narrower interval for the root.
Using $f(x)=\ln x-2+x$, which changes sign between $x=1$ and $x=2$, evaluate $f(1.5)$ and give a narrower interval for the root.
The equation $x^3-4x-2=0$ rearranges to $x=\sqrt[3]{4x+2}$. Using $x_0=2$, find $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$, to four decimal places.
The equation $x^2-5x+2=0$ rearranges to $x=5-\dfrac{2}{x}$. Using $x_0=4$, find $x_1$ and $x_2$, to four decimal places.
The equation $x^3-2x-5=0$ rearranges to $x=\sqrt[3]{2x+5}$. Using $x_0=2$, find $x_1$, to four decimal places.
Explain why the iteration $x_{n+1}=x_n^3-3$ (i.e. $g(x)=x^3-3$), starting from $x_0=1.5$, would fail to converge to a root of $x^3-x-3=0$ near $x=1.5$.
questions.answer: $g'(x)=3x^2$. At $x=1.5$: $g'(1.5)=3(2.25)=6.75$. Since $|g'(1.5)|=6.75>1$, the iteration does not satisfy the convergence condition $|g'(x)|<1$ near this point, so it diverges rather than converging to the root.

questions.q: Using $g(x)=5-\dfrac{2}{x}$ from the earlier iteration, find $g'(x)$ and evaluate $|g'(x)|$ at $x=4.56$ (near the root), to explain why the iteration converges there.
questions.answer: $g(x)=5-2x^{-1}$, so $g'(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2}$. At $x=4.56$: $g'(4.56)=\dfrac{2}{20.7936}\approx0.0962$. Since $|g'(4.56)|<1$, the iteration converges near this root.

questions.q: Rearrange $x^2-3x-1=0$ into the form $x=g(x)$ by making the linear term the subject.
Rearrange $x^3+x-1=0$ into the form $x=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}$, and verify algebraically that this is equivalent to the original equation.
questions.answer: From $x^3+x-1=0$: $x(x^2+1)=1$, so $x=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}$. Verifying: multiplying both sides by $(x^2+1)$ gives $x(x^2+1)=1$, i.e. $x^3+x=1$, i.e. $x^3+x-1=0$, which matches the original equation exactly.

questions.q: Use one iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, $x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$, with $x_0=2$ to find $x_1$ for $f(x)=x^3-4x-2$, to four decimal places.
Continuing from $x_1=2.25$ in the previous problem, find $x_2$, to four decimal places.
Use the Newton-Raphson method with $x_0=2.5$ to find $x_1$ for $f(x)=x^2-7$ (approximating $\sqrt{7}$), to four decimal places.
Use the Newton-Raphson method with $x_0=2$ to find $x_1$ for $f(x)=x^3-2x-5$, to four decimal places.

sections.heading: Further Newton-Raphson: rapid convergence and failure cases

questions.q: Using $x_1=2.65$ from the previous problem for $f(x)=x^2-7$, perform a second iteration to find $x_2$, to four decimal places, and compare with $\sqrt{7}\approx2.6458$.
questions.answer: $f(2.65)=7.0225-7=0.0225$. $f'(2.65)=5.3$. $x_2=2.65-\dfrac{0.0225}{5.3}\approx2.65-0.00425\approx2.6458$, matching $\sqrt{7}$ to four decimal places after just two iterations.

questions.q: Explain why $x_0=1$ is an unsuitable starting point for the Newton-Raphson method applied to $f(x)=x^3-3x+1$.
questions.answer: $f'(x)=3x^2-3$. At $x_0=1$: $f'(1)=3-3=0$. Since $f'(1)=0$, the tangent line at $x_0=1$ is horizontal and never meets the $x$-axis, so the formula $x_1=x_0-\dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}$ involves division by zero — the method fails at this starting point.

questions.q: Continuing from $x_1=2.1$ for $f(x)=x^3-2x-5$, perform a second Newton-Raphson iteration to find $x_2$, to four decimal places.
A root of $f(x)=x^3-4x-2$ lies in $(2.21,2.22)$, since $f(2.21)\approx-0.046$ and $f(2.22)\approx0.061$. State the midpoint estimate and the maximum possible error.
questions.answer: Midpoint: $\dfrac{2.21+2.22}{2}=2.215$. Maximum possible error: half the interval width, $\dfrac{2.22-2.21}{2}=0.005$.

questions.q: Given that the root of $f(x)=x^3-4x-2$ is trapped in the interval $(2.2141,2.2144)$ after further bisection, state the root correct to three decimal places, justifying your answer.
questions.answer: Every value in the interval $(2.2141,2.2144)$ rounds to $2.214$ at three decimal places (since both endpoints lie strictly between $2.2135$ and $2.2145$). The root is therefore $2.214$ to three decimal places.

questions.q: A root of $f(x)=x^3-2x-5$ lies in $(2.09,2.10)$, since $f(2.09)\approx-0.051$ and $f(2.10)\approx0.061$. State the midpoint estimate and the maximum possible error.
questions.answer: Midpoint: $\dfrac{2.09+2.10}{2}=2.095$. Maximum possible error: $\dfrac{2.10-2.09}{2}=0.005$ (consistent with the Newton-Raphson estimate $x_2\approx2.0946$ found earlier).

sections.heading: A well-designed word problem: designing a support strut

questions.q: This question has four parts. An engineer models the cross-sectional profile of a support strut by $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x-2$ (metres) and needs to find where it crosses the $x$-axis. (a) Show by a change of sign that a root lies between $x=0$ and $x=1$. (b) Use the Newton-Raphson method with $x_0=0.5$ to find $x_1$, to four decimal places. (c) Perform a second iteration to find $x_2$, to four decimal places. (d) Perform a third iteration to find $x_3$, and state the root to three decimal places.
